11. Reusable studies and standalone verbs

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-11-parameters.Rmd
book-11-parameters.Rmd

What you will learn

Bind typed parameters, use omop_study and shortcuts, then derive and filter columns without bringing rows to your computer.

You need: the client packages and the Opal login from Getting started. This chapter uses omop.synthea, the public synthetic Synthea27Nj data.

Start this chapter

Log in first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.synthea", server = "site")$conns

The connection is ready; conns identifies the server used by the analysis calls.

Describe the setting as a parameter

A parameter is a named, typed placeholder in a study definition. It lets you reuse a recipe without editing its logic. It is not R code or SQL text.

setting <- omop_param("setting", type = "concept_set")
setting
#> omop_param 'setting' (concept_set)

This parameter accepts concept sets. A separate date parameter would declare a date type; give each changing input its own appropriate type.

Build a template 

template <- omop_study(omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = setting),
  outputs = "baseline", baseline = list(
    prior_visits = omop_count("visit_occurrence", window = omop_window(-365, -1)),
    age = omop_age_at("index")))
recipe_params(template)
#> $setting
#> omop_param 'setting' (concept_set)

omop_study() returns an ordinary recipe. It creates an indexed population and baseline output. We explicitly exclude day zero from the prior-visit count. The parameter list shows that setting still needs a concept set. Compilation refuses an unbound template:

recipe_to_plan(template)
#> Error:
#> ! Unbound parameter 'setting' in the recipe; bind it with recipe_bind() before recipe_to_plan().

The error names setting and asks you to bind it. The template defines how to select people, but has not yet chosen which visit setting starts the study.

Bind and inspect 

outpatient <- recipe_bind(template, setting = 9202L)
recipe_params(outpatient)
#> list()

The empty parameter list means the bound copy has no remaining placeholders. Binding preserves the original template. Concept 9202 is the Outpatient Visit setting, found in chapter 4. Inpatient Visit is 9201. These select setting, not the record’s provenance type.

recipe_execute(outpatient, out = c(baseline = "D_param_outpatient"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_param_outpatient$age", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>    5%   10%   25%   50%   75%   90%   95%  Mean
#>  0.00  0.00  0.00  2.50 17.00 18.00 18.00  7.75
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_param_outpatient$age", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 0

The server computes completed age at the first outpatient visit. The median is 2.5 years, reflecting that many first visits in this synthetic life history occur in childhood. ds.numNA() reports no missing age: all 28 people contribute.

Read the simple-layer defaults 

explanation <- recipe_explain(outpatient)$text
writeLines(grep("^Population|^Output|^  (prior_visits|age):", explanation, value = TRUE))
#> Population 'study' (index): index = event 'visit_occurrence_9202', select = "first", end = observation_end
#>   prior_visits: count of event 'visit_occurrence' over days [-365, -1] relative to index
#>   age: age_at
#> Output 'baseline' [wide] rows 'study', grain episode

The short explanation identifies the population, prior-visit count, completed age and baseline output. The study’s default index selection is first. The population uses the default coverage policy; all requirements are combined with AND. Baseline has episode rows. For survival, supply outcomes and an explicit follow-up definition. For example, follow_up = list(start = 1, end = 365, censor = c("observation_end", "death")) describes a year after entry, ending sooner at a listed censor. The output chapter executes the corresponding native survival format.

Shortcuts expand into ordinary variables

Use a shortcut when its defaults match your question; use an explicit reducer when you need more control. before = 365 includes day zero, while after = 365 starts at day one. Without either, most shortcuts use all history through entry.

Chapter 4 identifies blood hemoglobin as 3000963 and gram per deciliter as 8713.

shortcuts <- omop_study(omop_event("measurement", 3000963L), outputs = "baseline",
  baseline = list(ever = omop_ever("measurement", 3000963L, before = 365),
    count = omop_count("measurement", 3000963L, before = 365),
    value = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3000963L,
      tolerance = c(-30, 0), unit = 8713L)))
recipe_execute(shortcuts, out = c(baseline = "D_shortcuts"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_shortcuts$ever",
  useNA = "no", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_shortcuts$ever
#>  1
#> 28

All 28 people have ever = 1 because the index hemoglobin measurement itself is included. To ask about measurements strictly before entry use window = omop_window(-365, -1) instead. First/last/mean/min/max-value shortcuts use the same event and window model. omop_history() bundles named ever variables; it does not define a new language.

Create columns on an assigned table

ds.omop.mutate() creates or replaces columns on a private omop.table. Although its notation looks like R, the client sends a mutate data request: the server validates a closed grammar and column types. It never runs arbitrary R code. Bare names refer to columns, including earlier assignments in the same call; literal numbers, strings, booleans and missing values are allowed.

The grammar supports +, -, *, /, comparisons of a column with a literal, ifelse, case_when, coalesce, and cut with public breaks. Date subtraction returns days; adding an integer to a date returns a date. Division by zero or nonfinite arithmetic gives missing values. Person, episode and set keys and other protected columns cannot be read or written; class-1 source names are also refused. Privacy explains those protections.

For derivation inside a new recipe, prefer the named formulas taught in Derived numeric formulas. This chapter deliberately teaches standalone mutation of an already assigned table, including sequential assignments, new objects and rollback. Those remain useful operations.

Prepare weight and height at the same date

BMI is weight in kilograms divided by squared height in metres. Index each person at their first weight measurement, then select weight and height on that date. We require the recorded kg and cm units; we do not combine unrelated latest readings or silently substitute a height from another day.

Look up the four inputs so that their names and IDs are visible together:

body_concepts <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(c(3025315L, 3036277L, 9529L, 8582L), conns = conns)
body_concepts$pooled[c("concept_id", "concept_name")]
concept_id concept_name
9529 kilogram
8582 centimeter
3025315 Body weight
3036277 Body height

Weight is 3025315, height 3036277, kilogram 9529, and centimeter 8582. These IDs identify the measurements and units used below.

weight_event <- omop_event("measurement", 3025315L)
body <- omop_study(weight_event, outputs = "baseline", baseline = list(
  weight_kg = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3025315L,
    tolerance = c(0, 0), unit = 9529L),
  height_cm = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3036277L,
    tolerance = c(0, 0), unit = 8582L),
  age = omop_age_at(omop_anchor(weight_event)),
  first_date = omop_date(omop_anchor(weight_event, which = "first")),
  last_date = omop_date(omop_anchor(weight_event, which = "last"))))
recipe_execute(body, out = c(baseline = "D_body"), conns = conns)

These are synthetic Synthea measurements, including children. Calculated BMI is a numeric teaching example, not an adult clinical classification.

Create a new object 

ds.omop.mutate("D_body", height_m = height_cm / 100,
  bmi = weight_kg / (height_m * height_m), newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 11.53374 13.62216 15.88957 23.86380 27.93787 30.20849 30.36386 22.11315
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 0

The mean BMI is 22.11 kg/m² across 28 people with no missing result. The second assignment uses the newly created height_m. A missing input gives a missing BMI. newobj = "D_bmi" preserves D_body; neither table is downloaded.

body_columns <- dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_body", datasources = conns)
bmi_columns <- dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_bmi", datasources = conns)
setdiff(bmi_columns$site, body_columns$site)
#> [1] "height_m" "bmi"

height_m and bmi are the two columns added to the new table. The source table still has its original columns.

Group ages with public breaks

Choose boundaries from the study design, not from private minimum/maximum ages. These broad age bands are for teaching. right = FALSE includes the lower bound and excludes the upper bound; ages outside the range remain missing.

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", age_group = cut(age, c(0, 18, 121),
  labels = c("under 18", "18 to 120"), right = FALSE),
  newobj = "D_grouped", conns = conns)
age_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_grouped$age_group",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
age_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_grouped$age_group
#> 18 to 120  under 18        NA
#>        14        14         0

There are 14 people under 18 and 14 aged 18–120 at their first weight. cut produces text labels in this grammar, not an ordered R factor. The table may display them alphabetically. Chapter 14 shows how to assign an explicit factor level sequence for modelling and display.

Exercise: create an adult flag using the same lower boundary of 18.

Solution — an age recode

ds.omop.mutate("D_grouped", adult = ifelse(age >= 18, "yes", "no"),
  newobj = "D_adults", conns = conns)
adult_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_adults$adult", useNA = "always",
  datasources = conns)
adult_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_adults$adult
#>  no yes  NA
#>  14  14   0

A missing age stays missing rather than becoming “no”. The 14 adults match the 18-to-120 band; the 14 under-18s become “no”.

Subtract dates on the server 

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", span_days = last_date - first_date,
  newobj = "D_span", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_span$span_days", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#>  952.700 1845.200 6142.500 6678.000 6996.500 7049.000 7053.550 5679.607

The mean span is 5,679.61 days and the median is 6,678 days across 28 people. This is elapsed time between first and last recorded weights, in days. It is not age or duration under continuous observation. Exact dates stay private.

Exercise: express that duration in 365-day years, retaining the days column.

Solution — convert a duration

ds.omop.mutate("D_span", span_years = span_days / 365,
  newobj = "D_years", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_years$span_years", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>        5%       10%       25%       50%       75%       90%       95%      Mean
#>  2.610137  5.055342 16.828767 18.295890 19.168493 19.312329 19.324795 15.560568

The mean is 15.56 years and the median is 18.30 years. Each summary is the day summary divided by 365. These are fixed-length units, not completed birthdays; use omop_age_at for completed age.

Recode with case_when

Cases are checked in order. The first true condition wins. In mutate, an unknown condition gives a missing result immediately, rather than falling through to the default. Handle missingness explicitly when your study needs it.

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", life_stage = case_when(
  is.na(age) ~ "unknown", age < 5 ~ "young child",
  age < 18 ~ "older child", .default = "adult"),
  newobj = "D_stage", conns = conns)
stage_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_stage$life_stage",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
stage_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_stage$life_stage
#>       adult older child young child          NA
#>          14           5           9           0

There are 9 young children, 5 older children and 14 adults. The declared default applies only after the preceding conditions are false. This recode distinguishes unknown age from a known age; it does not impute age.

To recode a derived text category, combine both child labels as follows:

ds.omop.mutate("D_stage", adult = case_when(
  life_stage %in% c("young child", "older child") ~ "no",
  life_stage == "unknown" ~ NA,
  .default = "yes"), newobj = "D_recoded", conns = conns)
recode_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_recoded$adult", useNA = "always",
  datasources = conns)
recode_counts$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_recoded$adult
#>  no yes  NA
#>  14  14   0

These counts agree with the earlier adult flag. Here the synthetic source has complete ages, so the missingness branch introduces no extra category count.

Replace an object in place

Use the same name for x and newobj to replace that server object. Omitting newobj instead generates a fresh name; it does not mean “in place”.

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", height_m = height_cm / 100,
  bmi = weight_kg / (height_m * height_m), bmi_copy = bmi,
  newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns)
before_columns <- dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_bmi", datasources = conns)
before_bmi <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_bmi$bmi", type = "combine", datasources = conns)
setdiff(before_columns$site, bmi_columns$site)
#> [1] "bmi_copy"

The replacement adds bmi_copy to the same named object. Failed assignments must leave the previous object usable; the next example checks that behaviour.

Read the refusal messages

The following failures are intentional. First try an unknown function:

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", bmi = sqrt(bmi), newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! ds.omop.mutate(): 'sqrt' is not part of the mutation grammar (+ - * /, conditions, ifelse, case_when, coalesce, cut, as.Date).

sqrt is outside the closed grammar and is refused by the client before a request can alter the table. Use supported arithmetic or a documented analysis function; arbitrary R functions cannot be sent through mutate.

Next try to copy a protected key. The server refuses this column reference:

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", copied = person_id,
  newobj = "D_key_copy", conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! OMOP mutate failed and was rolled back: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: column 'person_id' is a protected identifier and cannot be used in an expression; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

The message refuses the protected person key. Next, a class-1 source name is refused even as the name of a new column:

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", person_source_value = "label",
  newobj = "D_blocked_copy", conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! OMOP mutate failed and was rolled back: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: 'person_source_value' is a blocked (class-1) column name; choose another name; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

This is a blocked source/assignment name, not a request to alter its protection. Use descriptive study-variable names for allowed derived values.

Finally request an ordinary BMI change followed by a protected-key overwrite in the same in-place call. The whole request must fail:

ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", bmi = bmi + 1, person_id = "replacement",
  newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! OMOP mutate failed and 'D_bmi' was left unchanged: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: 'person_id' is a protected identifier and cannot be written; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors()

The protected-identifier message applies to person, episode and set keys and any columns marked protected by the server. It prohibits both reads and writes. Renaming a key is not an allowed transformation.

after_bmi <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_bmi$bmi", type = "combine", datasources = conns)
data.frame(
  State = c("Before refused change", "After refused change"),
  Mean_BMI = c(before_bmi$Global.Mean[1, "EstimatedMean"],
    after_bmi$Global.Mean[1, "EstimatedMean"]))
State Mean_BMI
Before refused change 22.11
After refused change 22.11

Both released means are 22.11. The earlier bmi + 1 in the refused request did not raise the mean by one. This aggregate check demonstrates that the failed request left the original numeric result available.

Filter using a predicate

A predicate is a condition. Only TRUE rows survive; missing conditions are dropped. This retains adults without using a key to target a known person.

ds.omop.filter("D_bmi", expr = omop_where(age >= 18),
  newobj = "D_adult_bmi", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_adult_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 14
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 22.75976 23.69819 25.78897 28.03959 29.79277 30.36457 30.45801 27.34679
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_adult_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 0

The 14 adults have a mean BMI of 27.35 kg/m², with no missing BMI. The subset meets the server’s distinct-person release threshold. It remains a private table. A small or empty final subset can be refused, as chapter 12 demonstrates.

A text-category predicate can select the same adults:

ds.omop.filter("D_stage", expr = omop_where(life_stage == "adult"),
  newobj = "D_working_age", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_working_age$bmi", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "numeric"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 14
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean
#> 22.75976 23.69819 25.78897 28.03959 29.79277 30.36457 30.45801 27.34679

This category means ages 18 and over, so its summary agrees with the preceding filter. The earlier missingness case ensures an unknown age is not called adult.

Exercise: change the index setting

Bind the same template to inpatient visits and summarise the prior-visit count. Do not alter the outpatient template in place.

Solution

inpatient <- recipe_bind(template, setting = 9201L)
recipe_execute(inpatient, out = c(baseline = "D_param_inpatient"), conns = conns)
inpatient_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_param_inpatient$prior_visits",
  type = "combine", datasources = conns)
inpatient_mean$Global.Mean
EstimatedMean Nmissing Nvalid Ntotal
studiesCombined 6.285714 0 7 7

The mean prior-visit count is 6.29 among the inpatient entrants. This is a separate bound recipe: its index changes which earlier visits are in the window. There are only seven entrants, so avoid quantiles that could expose individual values in such a small group; the mean is sufficient for this comparison.

Recap

Parameters change declared inputs, shortcuts express common native recipes, and mutate/filter operate privately on assigned tables. Each final object still passes the server’s release checks.
